lead: Laser action turns a pumped gain medium into an oscillator. Three things must happen together: the pump must create population inversion so stimulated emission beats absorption; mirrors must feed light back through the medium; and the pump must be strong enough to cross a threshold where round-trip gain equals round-trip loss. Below threshold the device behaves like an LED. Above threshold it emits narrow-linewidth, coherent light. Fiber links use this for long-haul transmitters, where launch power and spectral width matter. This chapter gives the conditions; 3.4 builds the diode.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for stimulated emission, 3.2 for recombination, and the idea of standing waves and modes from fiber propagation.

blocks.text: At thermal equilibrium, N<sub>2</sub>/N<sub>1</sub> = exp[−(E<sub>2</sub>−E<sub>1</sub>)/(k<sub>B</sub>T)], where k<sub>B</sub> is the Boltzmann constant (1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K) and T is the absolute temperature in kelvin. The lower level N<sub>1</sub> is fuller, so absorption beats stimulated emission. A pump lifts atoms to an upper level. A metastable upper level holds them long enough for a photon to arrive. Population inversion means N<sub>2</sub> > N<sub>1</sub>. Then stimulated emission exceeds absorption and the medium has gain. A semiconductor uses carrier density and quasi-Fermi levels instead of two discrete levels, but the test is the same: pump the active region until stimulated emission beats absorption. Only a few universities teach the full derivation; exams ask the condition and the gain formula.

blocks.where: g is gain per unit length (cm⁻¹); σ is the stimulated-emission cross-section (cm²); N<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>1</sub> are populations per unit volume (cm⁻³). Both N values are densities, not total counts.

blocks.text: Gain alone gives a single-pass amplifier. A Fabry-Perot cavity puts two mirrors around the gain medium and sends light back and forth. At threshold, round-trip gain equals total loss: R1R2·exp[2L(Γg<sub>th</sub> − α<sub>i</sub>)] = 1, so the light returns to its starting point with the same power. Taking the natural log of both sides gives the formula below. Above threshold gain clamps and extra pump becomes output. The cavity also selects longitudinal modes: 2nL = mλ, where n is refractive index, λ is vacuum wavelength and m is an integer. Mode spacing is Δν = c/(2n<sub>g</sub>L), with c the speed of light and n<sub>g</sub> the group index (n<sub>g</sub> ≈ n far from band edges). Threshold current is the pump current where the gain condition is first met. Threshold current density falls with lower α<sub>i</sub>, longer L, higher R<sub>1</sub>R<sub>2</sub>, or higher Γ. For a fixed stripe width the total threshold current still rises with L, because the pumped volume grows. This is why laser diodes confine light and carriers tightly.

Γ is the confinement factor (fraction of the mode in the gain medium); g<sub>th</sub> is threshold material gain (cm⁻¹); α<sub>i</sub> is internal loss (cm⁻¹); L is cavity length (cm); R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub> are mirror power reflectances (dimensionless).

spec.aria: A Fabry-Perot cavity: two mirror facets with reflectance 0.32, 300 micrometres apart, with arrows bouncing between them and output leaving both ends. Below, a bar from 0 to 50 per centimetre: internal loss 10 and mirror loss 37.98, total 47.98 per centimetre threshold modal gain.

examples.question: A Fabry-Perot semiconductor laser has L = 300 μm, R1 = R2 = 0.32, internal loss α<sub>i</sub> = 10 cm⁻¹ and confinement factor Γ = 0.30. Find the threshold modal gain and threshold material gain. Also find the longitudinal mode spacing in frequency for group index n<sub>g</sub> = 3.6.
steps: Threshold modal gain Γg<sub>th</sub> = α<sub>i</sub> + mirror loss = 10 + 37.98 = 47.98 cm⁻¹.
Mode spacing: Δν = c/(2n<sub>g</sub>L) = 3.00×10⁸/(2 × 3.6 × 300×10⁻⁶ m) = 1.389×10¹¹ Hz = 139 GHz. At 1.3 µm this is Δλ = λ²Δν/c = 0.78 nm.
examples.answer: Threshold modal gain is 47.98 cm⁻¹, threshold material gain is 159.94 cm⁻¹, and the modes are 139 GHz apart.
examples.check:
import math
L_um = 300.0
L_cm = L_um * 1e-4
R1 = 0.32
R2 = 0.32
alpha_i = 10.0
Gamma = 0.30
mirror_loss = (1.0/(2.0*L_cm)) * math.log(1.0/(R1*R2))
modal_gain = alpha_i + mirror_loss
material_gain = modal_gain / Gamma
print(f"{modal_gain:.2f}")
print(f"{material_gain:.2f}")

traps: Mixing centimetres and metres in 1/(2L): convert L to the unit of α<sub>i</sub> first. In the example, 300 μm = 0.03 cm.
Forgetting Γ: the threshold condition limits modal gain Γg<sub>th</sub>, so material gain is g<sub>th</sub> = Γg<sub>th</sub>/Γ.
Using R instead of R1R2: mirror loss needs the product, not one mirror.
Calling any strong pump inversion: inversion requires N2 > N1, not merely a large N2.
Saying gain grows without limit above threshold: gain clamps near threshold and extra pump becomes output.

quiz.q: State the condition for population inversion.
quiz.a: N₂ > N₁; more atoms sit in the upper laser level than the lower.
It returns photons through the gain medium so one pass adds gain repeatedly; without it, the device is only an amplifier.

quiz.q: A cavity has L = 0.05 cm, α<sub>i</sub> = 5 cm⁻¹, R₁ = R₂ = 0.30, Γ = 0.20. Find Γg<sub>th</sub>.
Why does threshold current fall when Γ rises?
quiz.a: Higher Γ means more of the mode overlaps the gain region, so a smaller material gain reaches the same modal gain; less pump current is needed.

quiz.q: What selects longitudinal modes in a Fabry-Perot cavity?
quiz.a: The round-trip phase condition 2nL = mλ; only wavelengths satisfying it resonate.

quiz.q: In worked example 1 the rear facet is coated so that R2 = 0.90, while R1 stays 0.32. Find the new mirror loss and Γg<sub>th</sub>.
quiz.a: R1R2 = 0.288; ln(1/0.288) = 1.245; α<sub>m</sub> = 1.245/(2 × 0.03 cm) = 20.75 cm⁻¹; Γg<sub>th</sub> = 10 + 20.75 = 30.75 cm⁻¹, down from 47.98 cm⁻¹. Most light now leaves through the uncoated front facet.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real transmitters use distributed feedback or distributed Bragg reflector gratings to pick one longitudinal mode; vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers use tiny cavities and high-reflectance mirrors. Quantum-well and quantum-dot active regions lower threshold current. Researchers study gain switching and mode locking for short pulses. Search: DFB laser threshold, VCSEL, longitudinal mode spacing.
